newsitem.title: INDIA: Philippines' Ramos eyes Indian technology, trade.
newsitem.headline: Philippines' Ramos eyes Indian technology, trade.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos said on Monday his country was seeking military equipment and technology from India under a 15-year plan to modernise its armed forces.

"There has been talk of (the) possibility of (the purchase of) small naval craft, and infantry or small arms equipment in which India is recognised," Ramos told reporters after holding talks with Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
Ramos, who arrived on Sunday on the first visit by a Philippine head of state to India since former president Ferdinand Marcos's visit in 1976, said he saw a bigger role for India in Asian affairs.
"There have been meetings already at the highest defence and military levels. The Philippines sees India as a potential source not so much of hardware or end items as of technology," Ramos said.
"For its part, the Philippines also can provide items for counter trade in order to facilitate business exchange."

Philippines Trade and Industry Secretary Cesar Bautista, who is accompanying Ramos, signed two cooperation agreements with Indian officials, one on science and technology, the other to boost small industries.
On Monday, Ramos, leading a business delegation of more than 80 people, attended a reception given by President Shankar Dayal Sharma at the presidential palace.
"We see India will be playing a much bigger role in the (Asian) region," Ramos told reporters at the palace.

"We acknowledged our common strategic interest in India's engagement in the affairs of East Asia, indeed on the forging of stronger links beween East Asia and South Asia," Ramos said in a statement issued later after bilateral talks.

Recalling Manila's support last year for New Delhi's participation in the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) dialogue process and the ASEAN Regional Forum, Ramos said he reiterated to Deve Gowda the Philippines' endorsement of India's membership in the Asia-Europe Meeting (ASEM).

"We had a very productive exchange of views on regional political matters, including recent developments in the Indian sub-continent, the Korean peninsula, the South China Sea, ASEAN and South-East Asia and the role of outside powers in the region," Ramos said.
He said he also discussed nuclear non-proliferation, curbing the use of landmines and other questions related to disarmament with Deve Gowda. He gave no further details.
Ramos said economic liberalisation in India and Philippines had improved prospects of business relations.

He listed several potential areas for economic cooperation between the two countries, including pharmaceuticals, information technology, energy, telecommunications, dairy, transportation, jewellery, garments and textiles.

"We explored measures to increase the flow of capital between our countries in the light of expanding opportunities for investments in both our economies," he said. "We expect several private sector agreements during this visit."
Philippines and India expected to double bilateral trade to $500 million by 2000 from the 1996 level of $250 million, Ramos said.
